#define OSD_COMPUTE_FACE_VARYING_2(result, fvarOffset, tessCoord)           {                                                                           vec2 v[4];                                                              int primOffset = OsdGetPatchIndex(gl_PrimitiveID) * 4;                  for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {                                               int index = (primOffset+i)*OSD_FVAR_WIDTH + fvarOffset;                 v[i] = vec2(texelFetch(OsdFVarDataBuffer, index).s,                                 texelFetch(OsdFVarDataBuffer, index + 1).s);            }                                                                       result = mix(mix(v[0], v[1], tessCoord.s),                                           mix(v[3], v[2], tessCoord.s),                                           tessCoord.t);                                          }
#define OSD_COMPUTE_FACE_VARYING_3(result, fvarOffset, tessCoord)           {                                                                           vec3 v[4];                                                              int primOffset = OsdGetPatchIndex(gl_PrimitiveID) * 4;                  for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {                                               int index = (primOffset+i)*OSD_FVAR_WIDTH + fvarOffset;                 v[i] = vec3(texelFetch(OsdFVarDataBuffer, index).s,                                 texelFetch(OsdFVarDataBuffer, index + 1).s,                             texelFetch(OsdFVarDataBuffer, index + 2).s);            }                                                                       result = mix(mix(v[0], v[1], tessCoord.s),                                           mix(v[3], v[2], tessCoord.s),                                           tessCoord.t);                                          }

<p><b>Danger of Paint Corruption!</b></p><p>The transform between the blending colorspace '%1' and the working colorspace '%2' uses an approximation on the graphics card. This can introduce very noticeable quantization errors in your textures.
<p><b>Mari was brought to you by:</b></p>
<p><b>Note: </b><i>All pixels picked outside of Mari's Canvas shall pick from the desktop's 8bit screen buffer. This includes previews of floating point images. (To pick colors from 16/32 bit depth images, use the Image picker tab in the Color palette)</i></p>
<p><pre>
<p><ul><li>
<p>And the
<p>Color-space transform method used when performing<br/>flattening and baking on export.</p><ul><li>Accurate:<p>All color-space transforms are done on the CPU. This<br/>gives the most mathematically correct results but incurs<br/>a cost of decreasing the speed of export.</p></li><li>Fast:<p>All color-space transforms are done on the GPU. This<br/>maximizes the speed of export, but can introduce errors<br/>due to the math, in some cases, being an approximation to<br/>the true method.</p></li><li>Automatic:<p>Whether we use the CPU or GPU is decided on case by case<br/>basis, based on the accuracy of color-space transform itself.</p></li></ul>
<p>Colormapping method used by the color swatches and color<br/>pickers.</p><ul><li>Raw:<p>No colormapping is applied and the raw values are<br/>displayed.</p></li><li>Color Manager:<p>The color values are colormapped using the current color<br/>profile set on the color manager. This gives a precise<br/>match to the canvas and image viewers.</p></li><li>OCIO:<p>The color values are colormapped to the <b>Monitor</b><br/>colorspace set in the project settings. This can be used<br/>to give a close match to the canvas and image viewers<br/>without the addition of the more advanced options such as<br/>gain and gamma correction.</p></li></ul>
<p>Control how Canvas pixels are picked, pre or post color managment
<p>Control how to process the alpha channel</p><ul><li>Premultiply: Premultiply RGB values by the alpha channel</li><li>Leave: Leave the alpha channel</li><li>Remove: Remove the alpha channel</li></ul>
<p>Default colorspace for 16-bit<br/>or 32-bit channels, and reading<br/>and writing image files encoded<br/>with 16-bit or 32-bit floating<br/>point data like EXRs.</p>
<p>Default colorspace for 8-bit<br/>channels, and reading and writing<br/>image files encoded with 8-bit<br/>data like JPGs, PNGs or TIFFs.</p>
<p>Default colorspace for all color<br/>pickers, swatches, and image<br/>viewers.</p><p>You will typically want to select<br/>the same colorspace that your 8-bit<br/>color channels default to in order<br/>to achieve perceptually consistent<br/>picked colors when switching<br/>between channels of different bit<br/>depth and colorspaces.</p>
<p>Default colorspace for masks,<br/>heights, normals, depths and,<br/>generally, any non-color image<br/>or channel with <b>scalar</b> integer<br/>data.</p>
<p>Default colorspace for reading<br/>and writing image files which<br/>are encoded with 16-bit integer<br/>data like TIFFs.</p>
<p>Default for applying blending<br/>operations such as, comp of the<br/>paint buffer and the current<br/>paint target, blending between<br/>layers, and combining inputs in<br/>a merge node.</p><p>You will typically want to select<br/>the <b>Same As 8 bit Data</b> colorspace<br/>to get the same results as<br/>painting prior to Mari 3.0, and<br/>to get less banding artifacts<br/>when painting 8-bit channels and<br/>images.</p>
<p>Default for painting,<br/>lighting, applying filters,<br/>and other such operations.</p><p>You will typically want to<br/>select the same linear-based<br/>colorspace as your 16/32-bit<br/>float channels to get accurate<br/>results.</p>
<p>Default monitor colorspace for all<br/>user interface elements which are<br/>displaying color managed swatches,<br/>pickers and thumbnails.</p><p>This preference does not affect the<br/>canvas and image viewers, however<br/>it is recommended to ensure that<br/>the View Transform matches this<br/>colorspace.</p>
<p>Default monitor colorspace for all<br/>user interface elements which are<br/>displaying non-color managed(scalar)<br/>swatches, pickers and thumbnails.</p><p>This preference does not affect the<br/>canvas and image viewers, however it<br/>is recommended to ensure that the<br/><b>scalar</b> View Transform matches<br/>this colorspace.</p>
<p>If you want to return the roamed license early you will need to reconnect to the license server's network first.</p>
<p>License roaming allows you to check out a floating license from the server for a number of days. You can then take the machine off the network and keep running %1.</p>
<p>Method used to apply pressure sensitivity to the brush<br/>stroke.</p><ul><li>Tablet:<p>Pressure is controlled directly by the pen tip of the<br/>tablet being used. If the device doesn't provide pressure<br/>control then 100% pressure is applied.</p></li><li>Key:<p>Pressure is modified over a fixed time interval. Pressure<br/>is increased by holding the <b>Spacebar</b> down, and is<br/>decreased by releasing it.</p></li><li>Wheel:<p>Pressure is applied at a fixed value that can be increased<br/>or decreased by the mouse wheel or tablet touch ring.</p></li></ul>
<p>Method used when generating mip-maps for images</p><ul><li>Accurate:<p>Image data is linearized before down-sampling and then<br/>converted back into the native color-space. This gives<br/>the most mathematically correct results but incurs a cost<br/>of decreasing the speed of processes such as baking.</p></li><li>Fast:<p>No linearization is performed and the down-sampling is<br/>done in the native color-space of the image data. This<br/>maximizes the speed of processes such as baking, but can<br/>introduce errors due to the math being non-linear.</p></li></ul>

<p>Turn all colorspace conversions, for<br/>the project, on or off. When switched<br/>off all data will treated as raw, similar<br/>to how it was treated prior to Mari 3.0.</p>
<p>When reading image files from disk, this<br/>option detects the colorspace of the image<br/>from colorspace names found in the<br/>image's file name and path.</p>
<p>When the results of color-space transforms, applied to<br/>images, should be clamped to the 0 to 1 range.</p><ul><li>Off:<p>No clamping is applied to any image. Clamping can still<br/>occur in places like the paint through tool when either<br/>the paint buffer or target image set is 8bit.</p></li><li>Byte:<p>Clamping is only applied when the color-space transform<br/>is applied to images that are 8bit.</p></li><li>All:<p>Clamping is applied to all images regardless of bit depth.</p></li></ul>

Adotmacron
Adrian Frutiger designed Avenir in 1988, after years of having an interest in sans serif typefaces. In an interview with Linotype, he said he felt an obligation to design a linear sans in the tradition of Erbar and Futura, but to also make use of the experience and stylistic developments of the twentieth century. The word Avenir means 'future' in French and hints that the typeface owes some of its interpretation to Futura. But unlike Futura, Avenir is not purely geometric; it has vertical strokes that are thicker than the horizontals, an "o" that is not a perfect circle, and shortened ascenders. These nuances aid in legibility and give Avenir a harmonious and sensible appearance for both texts and headlines. In 2004 Adrian Frutiger and the type director of Linotype GmbH Akira Kobayashi reworked the Avenir and created the Avenir Next for the Platinum Collection. It includes new small caps, newly designed true italics, and a complete new range of  weights. Avenir Next is a versatile sans serif family, ready for large and complex projects from books to signage to advertising.
Adrian Frutiger, Akira Kobayashi
